objectives: Define values and name important moral values
Explain honesty, respect, responsibility, tolerance and hard work
Explain self-discipline and the effect of bad habits

blocks.md: **Values** are beliefs about what is right and good that guide behaviour. **Moral values** help people to live together peacefully. Important values include **honesty** (telling the truth, not stealing or cheating), **respect** (for people, their beliefs and property), **responsibility** (doing your duties), **tolerance** (accepting people who are different), **hard work**, **fairness**, **courage** and **solidarity** (helping each other).

blocks.caption: Three important values
blocks.alt: Three columns describing honesty, respect and responsibility.

blocks.title: Applying values
blocks.md:
- **Honesty**: do your own exam work; return lost money or books.
- **Respect**: greet elders, listen when others speak.
- **Responsibility**: do homework, keep promises, take care of younger ones.
- **Tolerance**: accept different languages, religions and customs.
- **Hard work**: study regularly, do not look for shortcuts.

**Self-discipline** means controlling your own behaviour and feelings and working towards goals. It helps you to study, to avoid bad company and to resist harmful habits such as lying, stealing, drug use or truancy. Good character is formed gradually in the family, at school, in the church or mosque and among friends. **Role models** — a respected parent, teacher or community member — show values in action.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Being honest is not the same as being rude: tell the truth with respect.
- Tolerance does not mean accepting harm to others; it means respecting differences peacefully.
- Values are not only taught in lessons: they are learned by practice every day.

blocks.title: Example 1: which value?
blocks.statement: A pupil finds 500 FCFA in the classroom and gives it to the teacher. Which value does this show?
steps: She does not keep what is not hers.
She tells the truth about the find.

blocks.title: Example 2: tolerance
blocks.statement: Two pupils speak different home languages and have different religions. How can they show tolerance?
steps: They respect each other's customs and beliefs.
They share and learn about each other.

objectives: Describe the flag, the motto and the anthem of Cameroon
Name the capital and National Day
Behave correctly when the flag is raised or the anthem is sung

blocks.md: A **national symbol** represents a country and unites its people. The most important symbols of Cameroon are the **flag**, the **coat of arms**, the **motto** and the **national anthem**. The **capital** is Yaoundé. The **National Day** is **20 May**. Another important date in the school calendar is **11 February**, Youth Day.

blocks.caption: The flag of Cameroon
blocks.alt: The flag with vertical bands of green, red and yellow and a yellow star on the red band.

blocks.title: The flag and motto
blocks.md: The **flag** has three vertical bands: **green**, **red** and **yellow** from left to right, with a **yellow star** in the middle of the red band. The **motto** is **'Peace – Work – Fatherland'**. These symbols stand for the unity of the nation and the ideals of its people.

The **national anthem** is a song for solemn occasions, such as raising the flag, national celebrations and school ceremonies. Its title is **'O Cameroon, Cradle of our Forefathers'**. When the flag is raised or the anthem is played we **stand still, stay silent, face the flag** and show respect. Pupils learn the words and sing them properly.

blocks.title: Why respect symbols?
blocks.md: Symbols remind people that they belong to one country, whatever their language, religion or region. Respecting them shows love for the country and for fellow citizens. Damaging, mocking or dishonouring them is disrespectful and may be punished by law. Flags are never allowed to touch the ground.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Learn the order of the colours: green, red, yellow (left to right); the star is on the red band.
- The motto has three words: Peace, Work, Fatherland.
- National Day (20 May) is not the same as Youth Day (11 February) or reunification day (1 October).

blocks.title: Example 1: describe the flag
blocks.statement: Describe the flag of Cameroon in one sentence.
steps: Green, red and yellow from left to right.
A yellow star on the red band.
blocks.answer: Three vertical bands, green, red, yellow, with a yellow star on the red band.

blocks.title: Example 2: respect
blocks.statement: What should a pupil do when the national anthem is played at a ceremony?
steps: Stand still and face the flag.
Show respect until the anthem ends.
blocks.answer: Stand still, be silent or sing, and show respect.

blocks.md: Every child has **rights**: things they are entitled to so that they can grow up healthy, safe and educated. In 1989 the United Nations adopted the **Convention on the Rights of the Child**, an international agreement which many countries, including Cameroon, have accepted. Its main ideas are survival, development, protection and participation.

items.text: Rights and duties of the child

blocks.caption: Rights and duties
blocks.alt: Two columns of rights and duties of a child.

blocks.title: Main rights of a child
blocks.md:
- To a **name** and a **nationality** (a birth certificate helps).
- To **life, food, shelter and health care**.
- To **education**.
- To **protection** from violence, abuse, exploitation and harmful child labour.
- To **play and rest**.
- To **express opinions** and be heard, according to age and maturity.
- To be cared for by parents, or to receive protection if there is no family.

blocks.title: Duties of a child
blocks.md: Respect parents, teachers and others; obey rules; study and attend school; help with household tasks; take care of property; protect the environment; and respect the rights of others. A child cannot demand rights while denying duties: each right is matched by responsibility, and the rights of others set limits on my own.

**Who protects children?** Parents and guardians first, then the school, the community, religious leaders, the health services, the police and courts, and government bodies, assisted by organisations such as UNICEF. A child who is hurt or abused should tell a trusted adult. Children should avoid dangers such as strangers who offer money or gifts, and should not be forced into marriage or dangerous work.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Having rights does not mean doing whatever you like.
- Discipline by parents must respect the child's dignity: abuse and cruelty are never acceptable.
- Rights apply to every child, whether girl or boy, rich or poor, disabled or not.

blocks.title: Example 1: right or duty?
blocks.statement: Classify: A) going to school; B) obeying school rules; C) receiving health care; D) helping at home.
steps: Education and health care are entitlements: rights.
Obeying rules and helping at home are responsibilities: duties.
So A and C are rights; B and D are duties.
blocks.answer: A and C rights; B and D duties.

blocks.title: Example 2: protection
blocks.statement: A child is beaten at home and is afraid. Whom can the child tell?
steps: The child can tell a trusted adult: a teacher, relative or religious leader.
Social services or the police can also help.
Telling is the first step towards protection.
blocks.answer: A trusted adult such as a teacher, a relative or social services.
